Lessons.Title: Mystery Computations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: use changing spreadsheet inputs to infer hidden formulas, validate rules with several trials, and write formulas referencing cells. Original Edulytiks adaptation of optional Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 6, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/6/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). This source emphasizes repeated reasoning MP8 rather than a numbered publisher Addressing target.

Independent spreadsheet model: cell B2 contains =A2+2*A3. With A2=5 and A3=4, it displays 13; with A2=7 and A3=4 it displays 15; with A2=5 and A3=6 it displays 17. Hiding the formula creates a rule-discovery task. Vary one input at a time; a single trial does not establish which formula is correct.

Student activity: use an actual accessible spreadsheet when available; experiment with zero, negative numbers and fractions to test the rule. Create =A2+A4 in B2, build a distinct mystery rule in B3, then exchange with a partner and justify a conjecture. A paper grid is a clearly labelled substitute when software is unavailable, not proof of interactive spreadsheet operation.

Teacher-scored rubric: 0–2 each for entering or describing a valid formula, using at least three contrasting trials, explaining the inferred relationship, and checking a counterexample (8 total). Unobserved clicking or partner discussion must never receive synthetic automatic credit.

V13 optionality and required medium: publisher U1L6 is part of an OPTIONAL three-lesson spreadsheet introduction. If students already know spreadsheets, an authorized teacher can skip the sequence; no school should record an unassigned optional task as failed. An internet-enabled spreadsheet is the original interaction, not a static arithmetic worksheet. No actual application operation or partner turn is evidenced by this content file.

V13 original Make-24 and cell-probe sequence: combine 1,3,4,6 with 6/(1-3/4)=24. In a live spreadsheet define B2 = A2+A4 and hold A3 constant while testing A2=5,A4=-2 (3); A2=-0.5,A4=0.75 (0.25); then change only A3 and explain why B2 does not move. Move to a new B3 formula and exchange hidden-rule input trials with another learner; explicitly distinguish a spreadsheet-run observation from a written hypothetical.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cell address
KeyConcepts.Definition: A spreadsheet reference such as A2 names a cell's current value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a column letter plus row number in formulas.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dynamic formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: Referenced formulas recompute after input changes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Change one value and predict a result.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rule conjecture
KeyConcepts.Definition: Finite input-output examples support a hypothesis but rarely prove it uniquely.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test inputs that distinguish competing rules.
KeyConcepts.Example: x+2 and 2x both give 4 at x=2 but differ at x=3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Infer a two-variable rule
WorkedExamples.Question: Given outputs 13,15,17 for inputs (5,4),(7,4),(5,6), propose a formula.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain each calculation and verify it independently.
Steps: Raising A2 by 2 raises output by 2, suggesting coefficient 1.
Raising A3 by 2 raises output by 4, suggesting coefficient 2.
WorkedExamples.Check: More trials are needed to distinguish all possible rules.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check negative and fractional inputs
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate =A2+2*A3 for A2=-3 and A3=1.5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain each calculation and verify it independently.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B2=0 initially, then 1 after A3 becomes 2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Create a partner formula
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate =3*A2-A4 at (A2,A4)=(4,5) and (0,-2).
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain each calculation and verify it independently.
WorkedExamples.Check: Signed subtraction is consistent in both cases.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating a cell address with its label
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A2 means the changing cell value, not the letters A2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inferring a rule from one example
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different rules can agree at a single point.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Vary each input in multiple trials.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Subtracting a negative adds a positive.

SummaryPoints: Cell references read changing data and formulas recalculate.
Vary one input at a time when inferring a hidden rule.
Test competing formulas with negative, zero and decimal inputs.
Teacher observation, not a numerical score, establishes actual spreadsheet interaction.

Visuals.Title: Original accessible numerical demonstration
Visuals.Description: Each row is explicitly labelled practice data, not real student observations.
